uncited: This method optimizes the data transfer and memory management overhead inherent in hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering.
It solves the problem of high latency caused by frequent, fragmented RAM-to-GPU transfers required to load visible Gaussians for each frame.

By storing Spherical Primitive Tree (SPT) properties in a continuous GPU buffer and transferring Gaussian properties via a single bulk copy operation followed by GPU-side reorganization, it minimizes PCIe bus traffic and kernel launch overhead.

It differs from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the hierarchical cut logic (handled via cached SPTs) from the rasterization-ready data layout (SoA), whereas methods like [Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling](2067-non-tiled-2d-gaussian-splatting-with-transmittance-culling.md) focus on pixel-level culling and [Opacity-Thresholded Tile Intersection Filtering](2109-opacity-thresholded-tile-intersection-filtering.md) focus on tile-level geometric filtering.
The method operates in two phases: the initial setup of memory buffers and the per-frame loading pipeline.
*   Current camera pose and view frustum.
**SPT Properties Buffer (GPU):** A single continuous GPU memory buffer storing hierarchical metadata.
**Gaussian Properties (CPU):** A single PyTorch tensor in RAM.
**Render Set (GPU):** The final Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout required by the tiled rasterizer.
**SPT Cut Execution:** The GPU performs the HSPT cut in parallel using optimized CUDA kernels.
This minimizes PCIe transfer overhead compared to individual element transfers.
**GPU Reorganization (AoS to SoA):** On the GPU, reorganize the transferred Gaussian properties from the incoming AoS layout into the SoA layout required by the rasterizer.
*   **Memory Thresholds:** VRAM usage is bounded by an LRU writeback policy.
This variant extends the basic loading optimization by caching SPT cuts in VRAM to avoid redundant RAM-to-GPU transfers for similar views.
For each training view, visible Gaussians are assembled from the upper hierarchy, cached SPTs, and skybox Gaussians (which remain in VRAM).
Newly loaded SPTs are added to the cache after each iteration.
An LRU policy bounds VRAM usage; when the threshold is exceeded, entries are written back to RAM.
*   **Time Complexity:** The cut operation is parallelized on the GPU.
The dominant cost is the RAM-to-GPU transfer, which is reduced from $O(N)$ fragmented transfers to $O(K)$ single bulk transfers, where $K$ is the number of visible Gaussians.
The AoS-to-SoA reorganization is $O(K)$ on the GPU.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Requires continuous GPU buffers for SPT properties and the render set.
*   **Strengths:** Significantly reduces PCIe bandwidth pressure; improves training stability through cache-induced stochasticity.
It addresses the scalability issues of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in large scenes, where the sheer number of Gaussians makes naive rendering and densification infeasible.

The approach builds on [3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced)](3369-gaussian-splatting-rendering.md) by introducing hierarchical memory management and optimized data layout transitions.
